title: De Opificio Dei
author: Lactantius

passages.original: in summo uero constructionis eius quam similem nauali carinae diximus. caput conlocauit, in quo esset regimen totius animantis, datumque illi hoc nomen est, ut quidem Varro ad Ciceronem scribit, quod hinc capiant initium sensus ac nerui.
passages.english: At the top of its structure, which we have said resembles the keel of a ship, he placed the head, in which the government of the whole living creature was to reside; and this name was given to it, as Varro indeed writes to Cicero, because from here the senses and the nerves take (capiant) their beginning.
passages.notes: The etymology plays on caput 'head' and capere 'take'. The full stop after 'diximus' in the printed text is treated as a mid-sentence pause.

passages.original: uerum alias refellemus Epicurum: nunc de prouidentia ut coepimus disseramus.
passages.english: But we shall refute Epicurus elsewhere; now let us discuss providence, as we began.

passages.original: ac primum quod oculorum orbes concauis foraminibus conclusit, a quo foratu frontem nominatam Varro existimat, eos neque minus neque amplius quam duos esse uoluit, quod ad speciem nullus est perfectior numerus quam duorum, sicut et aures duas: quarum duplicitas incredibile est quantam pulchritudinem praeferat, quod cum pars utraque similitudine ornata est, tum ut uenientes altrinsecus uoces facilius colligantur.
passages.english: And first, he enclosed the orbs of the eyes in hollow openings, and from this boring (foratus) Varro thinks the brow (frons) was named. He willed that there should be neither fewer nor more than two of them, because for beauty no number is more perfect than two, just as [he made] the ears two as well. It is incredible how much beauty their doubleness displays, both because each side is adorned by its likeness [to the other], and so that sounds coming from either side may be gathered more easily.
passages.notes: The etymology plays on foratus 'boring' and frons 'brow'.

passages.original: et idcirco mens ac uoluntas ex oculis saepe dinoscitur. quod quidem ut refelleret Lucretius, ineptissimo usus est argumento. si enim mens inquit per oculos uidet, erutis et effossis oculis magis uideret, quoniam euulsae cum postibus fores plus inferunt luminis quam si fuerint obductae.
passages.english: And for that reason the mind and will are often recognised from the eyes. To refute this, Lucretius used a most foolish argument. For if, he says, the mind sees through the eyes, it would see better with the eyes torn out and dug away, since doors wrenched off together with their posts let in more light than if they had been closed.

passages.original: nimirum ipsi uel potius Epicuro qui eum docuit effossi oculi erant, ne uideret effossos orbes et ruptas oculorum fibras et fluentem per uenas sanguinem et crescent- tes ex uulneribus carnes et obductas ad ultimum cicatrices nihil posse lucis admittere, nisi forte oculos auribus similes nasci uolebat, ut non tam oculis quam foraminibus cerneremus: quo nihil ad speciem foedius, ad usum inutilius fieri potest.
passages.english: Clearly it was he himself, or rather Epicurus who taught him, whose eyes had been dug out, so that he did not see that the gouged sockets, the torn fibres of the eyes, the blood flowing through the veins, the flesh growing from the wounds, and finally the scars drawn over them can let in no light at all. Unless perhaps he wanted eyes to be born like ears, so that we would see not so much with eyes as with holes: nothing could be uglier to look at, or more useless in function.
passages.notes: 'crescent- tes' is a scanning split for 'crescentes'.

passages.original: habet praeterea et aliud officium, quo in omnibus, non tamen solo in mutis utitur, quod contritos et permolitos dentibus cibos colligit et conglobatos ui sua deprimit et transmittit ad uentrem. itaque Varro a ligando cibo putat linguae nomen inpositum. bestias etiam <in> potu adiuuat:
passages.english: It also has another function, which it performs in all [creatures], though not only in the dumb animals: it gathers the food that has been crushed and ground by the teeth, rolls it into a ball, presses it down by its force and sends it on to the stomach. And so Varro thinks the name of the tongue (lingua) was given from binding (ligando) the food. It also helps beasts in drinking:
passages.notes: The etymology plays on ligare 'bind' and lingua 'tongue'. 'non tamen solo in mutis' is awkward as transmitted, and the sense may be corrupt. '<in>' is an editorial supplement.

passages.original: item mulier, ut Varro interpretatur, a mollitie, inmutata et detracta littera, uelut mollier. cui suscepto fetu cum partus adpropinquare iam coepit, turgescentes mammae dulcibus sucis distenduntur et ad nutrimenta nascentis fontibus lacteis fecundum pectus exuberat.
passages.english: Likewise 'woman' (mulier), as Varro explains it, [comes] from softness (mollitia), with a letter changed and [another] removed, as if 'mollier'. When she has conceived offspring and the birth has begun to draw near, her breasts swell and are distended with sweet juices, and her fruitful bosom overflows with fountains of milk for the nourishment of the newborn.
passages.notes: The etymology plays on mollitia 'softness' and mulier 'woman'.

passages.original: quid rienum gemina similitudo? quos ait Varro ita dictos. quod riui ab his obsceni umoris oriantur: quod est longe secus, quia spinae altrinsecus supini cohaerent et sunt ab intestinis separati. quid splenis? quid iecur?
passages.english: What of the twin likeness of the kidneys (renes)? Varro says they are so called because streams (rivi) of foul fluid arise from them. This is far from the case, because they cling on either side to the spine, lying on their backs, and are separated from the intestines. What of the spleen? What of the liver?
passages.notes: 'rienum' is an old form of 'renum'. The etymology plays on rivi 'streams' and renes 'kidneys'.

passages.original: illud autem caue ne umquam simile ueri putaueris quod Aristoxenus dicit, mentem omnino nullam esse, sed quasi harmoniam in fidibus ex constructione corporis et conpagibus uiscerum uim sentiendi existere. musici enim intentionem concentumque neruorum in integros modos sine ulla offensione consonantium harmoniam appellant.
passages.english: But beware of ever thinking that what Aristoxenus says is anything like the truth: that there is no mind at all, but that the power of sensation arises from the structure of the body and the joining of the organs, like harmony in the strings [of a lyre]. For musicians call the tension and concord of the strings into complete melodies, without any clash among the sounding notes, harmony.

passages.original: at illi qui uentum putant, hoc falluntur, quod ex aere spiritum ducentes uiuere uidemur. Varro ita definit: anima est aer conceptus ore, deferuefactus in pulmone, temperatus in corde, diffusus in corpus.
passages.english: But those who think [the soul] is wind are deceived in this, that we seem to live by drawing breath from the air. Varro defines it thus: the soul is air taken in by the mouth, heated in the lungs, tempered in the heart, and diffused into the body.
passages.notes: The subject 'the soul' (anima) is supplied from the definition that follows.

passages.original: haec apertissime falsa sunt. neque enim tam obscuram nobis huiusmodi rerum dico esse rationem, ut ne hoc quidem intellegamus, quid uerum esse non possit. an si mihi quispiam dixerit aeneum esse caelum aut uitreum aut, ut Empedocles ait, aerem glaciatum, statimne adsentiar, quia caelum ex qua materia sit ignorem? sicut enim hoc nescio, ita illud scio.
passages.english: These things are most plainly false. For I do not say that the account of such matters is so obscure to us that we cannot understand even this: what cannot be true. If someone were to tell me that the sky is made of bronze, or of glass, or, as Empedocles says, of frozen air, should I agree at once because I do not know of what material the sky is made? For just as I do not know that, so I do know this.

passages.original: quare neque semper uera sunt neque semper falsa, Vergilio teste, qui duas portas esse uoluit somniorum. sed quae falsa sunt, dormiendi causa uidentur, quae uera, inmittuntur a deo, ut imminens bonum aut malum hac reuelatione discamus.
passages.english: Therefore [dreams] are neither always true nor always false, as Virgil testifies, who held that there are two gates of dreams. But those that are false are seen for the sake of sleep; those that are true are sent by God, so that by this revelation we may learn of an impending good or evil.
passages.notes: The subject (dreams) is supplied from the wider context.

passages.original: itaque serendarum animarum ratio uni ac soli deo subiacet: denique caelesti sumus omnes semine oriundi,omnibus ille idem pater est, ut ait Lucretius. nam de mortalibus non potest quicquam nisi mortale generari. nec putari pater debet qui transfudisse <se> aut inspirasse animam de sua nullo modo sentit, nec si sentiat, quando tamen aut quomodo id fiat habet animo conprehensum.
passages.english: Thus the method of sowing souls lies with the one and only God: "in short, we are all sprung from heavenly seed; for all of us he is the same father," as Lucretius says. For from mortals nothing can be generated except what is mortal. Nor should he be thought a father who in no way perceives that he has transfused or breathed a soul from his own, nor, if he did perceive it, has grasped in his mind when or how it happens.
passages.notes: <se> is an editorial supplement: 'transfused himself'; rendered loosely with 'from his own'.
